body.heading: Attention has a cold start
paragraphs: Sitting down to work and expecting instant focus is like sprinting from the doorstep. The first minutes are usually scattered: stray thoughts, small urges to check things, a mind still chewing on the previous hour.
A short warm-up gives your attention a runway. Two or three minutes of something simple and absorbing tells your brain, kindly and clearly, that the mode is changing.

body.heading: Three warm-ups to try
paragraphs: The tidy two: spend two minutes clearing your workspace of everything unrelated to the task. You are not procrastinating; you are removing future distractions while they are still objects rather than temptations.

The first line: write, by hand, one sentence about what you are about to do and what “done for now” looks like. Or try the noticing minute: look out of the window and silently name everything you can see, hear and feel, until your mind slows to walking pace.

body.heading: Ritual beats intensity
paragraphs: The warm-up works best when it is the same each time. Sameness is what turns a random activity into a signal. Choose one, keep it short, and do it even — especially — on days when focus feels far away.
If you sit down and your mind still wanders, nothing has gone wrong. Wander, notice, return. That returning is the exercise, and every rep counts.

takeaway: Give your mind a two-minute runway before you ask it to fly.
